title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
short: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
author: Frederick Douglass
blurb: Frederick Douglass recounts his childhood in Talbot County, Maryland, learning to read in Baltimore, his fight with Covey, and his escape north to freedom in New Bedford.

title: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl
short: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl
author: Harriet Jacobs
blurb: Writing as Linda Brent, the author tells of her master's persecution, seven years hidden in a cramped garret, her escape north, and freedom at last for herself and her children.

title: Twelve Years a Slave: Narrative of Solomon Northup, a Citizen of New-York, Kidnapped in Washington City in 1841, and Rescued in 1853, from a Cotton Plantation near the Red River, in Louisiana
author: Solomon Northup
blurb: Solomon Northup, a free citizen of New York, was kidnapped in Washington in 1841 and held twelve years on Louisiana plantations near the Red River until his rescue in 1853.

title: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African
short: The Interesting Narrative of Olaudah Equiano
author: Olaudah Equiano
blurb: Equiano tells of his childhood in Eboe, his kidnapping and passage on a slave ship, years as an enslaved seaman, how he bought his freedom, and his later travels.

title: Running a Thousand Miles for Freedom; or, The Escape of William and Ellen Craft from Slavery
short: Running a Thousand Miles for Freedom
author: William and Ellen Craft
blurb: William and Ellen Craft escaped from slavery in Georgia in December 1848, Ellen disguised as an invalid gentleman with William as her slave, and later fled to England.

title: The History of Mary Prince, a West Indian Slave
author: Mary Prince
blurb: Mary Prince tells of her enslavement in Bermuda, at the salt ponds of Turk's Island and in Antigua, and of leaving her owners' household in London.

title: Narrative of Sojourner Truth
author: Sojourner Truth
blurb: Dictated by Sojourner Truth, the narrative follows Isabella from slavery in Ulster County, New York, through her escape, her lawsuit to recover her son, and her preaching travels.

title: My Bondage and My Freedom
author: Frederick Douglass
blurb: Douglass retells his Maryland childhood, enslavement and escape, then follows his life as an abolitionist lecturer, his twenty-one months in Great Britain, and his newspaper work, with speeches appended.

title: Up from Slavery: An Autobiography
author: Booker T. Washington
blurb: Booker T. Washington tells of his birth in slavery in Franklin County, Virginia, his schooling at Hampton, and his work building Tuskegee Institute in Alabama.

title: Narrative of William W. Brown, a Fugitive Slave
author: William Wells Brown
blurb: William Wells Brown describes slavery in Kentucky and Missouri, being hired out to a slave trader on the Mississippi, and his escape to Ohio, where a Quaker named him.

title: Narrative of the Life and Adventures of Henry Bibb, an American Slave
short: The Life and Adventures of Henry Bibb
author: Henry Bibb
blurb: Henry Bibb recounts slavery in Kentucky, his escapes and returns to rescue his wife and child, their sale together to the far South, and his life as a free lecturer.

title: The Fugitive Blacksmith; or, Events in the History of James W. C. Pennington, Pastor of a Presbyterian Church, New York, Formerly a Slave in the State of Maryland, United States
author: James W. C. Pennington
blurb: James W. C. Pennington, a blacksmith enslaved on Maryland's eastern shore, tells of his flight north, his capture and escape, Quaker friends in Pennsylvania, and his religious calling.

title: Behind the Scenes; or, Thirty Years a Slave, and Four Years in the White House
author: Elizabeth Keckley
blurb: Elizabeth Keckley recounts her girlhood in slavery in Virginia, buying freedom for herself and her son in St. Louis, and her years as Mrs. Lincoln's dressmaker and friend in Washington.

title: A Narrative of the Life and Adventures of Venture, a Native of Africa, but Resident above Sixty Years in the United States of America
short: The Life and Adventures of Venture
author: Venture Smith
blurb: Venture, son of a prince in Guinea, describes his capture as a child, his enslavement in New York and Connecticut, and buying freedom for himself and his family.

title: Narrative of the Life of Moses Grandy, Late a Slave in the United States of America
short: Narrative of the Life of Moses Grandy
author: Moses Grandy
blurb: Moses Grandy of Camden County, North Carolina, a canal boatman, tells how he paid for his freedom three times over before working to redeem his wife and children.

title: The Narrative of Lunsford Lane, Formerly of Raleigh, N.C., Embracing an Account of His Early Life, the Redemption by Purchase of Himself and Family from Slavery, and His Banishment from the Place of His Birth for the Crime of Wearing a Colored Skin
author: Lunsford Lane
blurb: Lunsford Lane of Raleigh, North Carolina, bought his freedom with money earned selling tobacco, then was banished from the state while trying to buy his wife and children.

title: Harriet, the Moses of Her People
short: Harriet, the Moses of Her People
author: Sarah H. Bradford
blurb: Sarah Bradford tells how Harriet Tubman escaped slavery in Maryland, returned south again and again to lead others out, and served the Union army as scout and nurse.

title: Twenty-Two Years a Slave, and Forty Years a Freeman; Embracing a Correspondence of Several Years, While President of Wilberforce Colony, London, Canada West
author: Austin Steward
blurb: Austin Steward recalls slavery on a Virginia plantation and in New York, his freedom and business life in Rochester, and his years leading the Wilberforce colony in Canada.

title: Thirty Years a Slave: From Bondage to Freedom; The Institution of Slavery as Seen on the Plantation and in the Home of the Planter
author: Louis Hughes
blurb: Louis Hughes, sold in Richmond as a boy, describes slavery on a Mississippi plantation and in Memphis, repeated escape attempts, his freedom during the war, and later life in Milwaukee.

title: A Slave Girl's Story: Being an Autobiography of Kate Drumgoold
author: Kate Drumgoold
blurb: Kate Drumgoold recalls a Virginia childhood in slavery, her mother's sale during the war and return, and her own schooling and years as a teacher.

title: Memories of Childhood's Slavery Days
author: Annie L. Burton
blurb: Annie L. Burton remembers her childhood on a plantation near Clayton, Alabama, during the Civil War and her life after freedom, followed by essays, poems and hymns.

title: From the Darkness Cometh the Light; or, Struggles for Freedom
short: From the Darkness Cometh the Light
author: Lucy A. Delaney
blurb: Lucy A. Delaney tells how her mother, a free woman kidnapped from Illinois into slavery, won her freedom in court and then sued in St. Louis to free her daughter.

title: The Story of Mattie J. Jackson; Her Parentage—Experience of Eighteen Years in Slavery—Incidents during the War—Her Escape from Slavery
short: The Story of Mattie J. Jackson
author: Mattie J. Jackson
blurb: Mattie J. Jackson describes slavery in St. Louis during the Civil War, her family's sales and escape attempts, and her own escape to freedom in Indianapolis.

title: Memoir of Old Elizabeth, a Coloured Woman
author: Old Elizabeth
blurb: Born a slave in Maryland in 1766, Elizabeth tells of her religious awakening, her freedom, and her many years travelling as a preacher before settling in Philadelphia.

title: A Narrative of the Life of Rev. Noah Davis, a Colored Man
short: The Life of Rev. Noah Davis
author: Noah Davis
blurb: Noah Davis, born a slave in Virginia, tells how he became a Baptist preacher, bought his own freedom, and worked in Baltimore to buy his wife and children.

title: Narrative of the Life of J. D. Green, a Runaway Slave, from Kentucky, Containing an Account of His Three Escapes, in 1839, 1846, and 1848
short: Narrative of the Life of J. D. Green
author: J. D. Green
blurb: J. D. Green tells of slavery in Maryland and his three escapes, in 1839, 1846 and 1848, the last of which brought him to freedom in Canada.

title: The Confessions of Nat Turner, the Leader of the Late Insurrections in Southampton, Va.
author: Nat Turner
blurb: In his cell, Nat Turner tells Thomas R. Gray of his visions and of the 1831 revolt he led in Southampton, Virginia; Gray adds the trial and court lists.

title: Wonderful Adventures of Mrs. Seacole in Many Lands
author: Mary Seacole
blurb: Mary Seacole of Kingston, Jamaica, tells of fighting cholera in Panama and of her British Hotel near Balaclava, where she fed and nursed soldiers during the Crimean War.

title: The Underground Rail Road: A Record of Facts, Authentic Narratives, Letters, &c.
author: William Still
blurb: William Still, chairman of Philadelphia's Acting Vigilance Committee, records the escapes of hundreds of fugitives it aided, with their letters, advertisements for runaways, and sketches of abolitionist helpers.

title: The Colored Cadet at West Point: Autobiography of Lieut. Henry Ossian Flipper, U.S.A., First Graduate of Color from the U.S. Military Academy
short: The Colored Cadet at West Point
author: Henry Ossian Flipper
blurb: Henry O. Flipper, born a slave in Georgia, recounts his four years of ostracism at West Point and his graduation in 1877 as the academy's first graduate of color.

title: Life and Times of Frederick Douglass, Written by Himself: His Early Life as a Slave, His Escape from Bondage, and His Complete History to the Present Time
short: Life and Times of Frederick Douglass
author: Frederick Douglass
blurb: Douglass’s third autobiography retells his slavery and escape, then follows the antislavery years, John Brown, recruiting Black regiments, Lincoln, Reconstruction and his public offices to 1881.

title: A Negro Explorer at the North Pole
short: A Negro Explorer at the North Pole
author: Matthew A. Henson
blurb: Matthew Henson, who served on Robert E. Peary's Arctic expeditions from 1891, describes the 1908–09 sledge journey across the polar sea that reached the North Pole.

title: A Narrative of the Uncommon Sufferings, and Surprizing Deliverance of Briton Hammon, a Negro Man,—Servant to General Winslow, of Marshfield, in New-England; Who Returned to Boston, after Having Been Absent Almost Thirteen Years
author: Briton Hammon
blurb: Briton Hammon, servant to General Winslow of Marshfield, tells of shipwreck on the Florida coast, captivity among Indians, years in a Havana dungeon, and his chance meeting with his old master in London.

title: The Blind African Slave, or Memoirs of Boyrereau Brinch, Nick-named Jeffrey Brace
author: Boyrereau Brinch
with: written down by Benjamin F. Prentiss
blurb: Boyrereau Brinch describes his boyhood in the kingdom of Bow-woo near the Niger, his kidnapping by English slavers, his sale in Barbadoes, service at sea and in the American army, emancipation and later life in Vermont, with long passages of scripture and comment by his amanuensis.

title: The Life, History, and Unparalleled Sufferings of John Jea, the African Preacher
short: The Life of John Jea, the African Preacher
author: John Jea
blurb: John Jea tells how he was stolen from Old Callabar as a child and enslaved in New York, how an angel, he says, taught him to read the Bible, and how he preached in America, Holland, England and France.

title: Life of William Grimes, the Runaway Slave. Written by Himself
short: Life of William Grimes, the Runaway Slave
author: William Grimes
blurb: William Grimes tells of slavery under a run of masters in Virginia and Georgia, his escape from Savannah stowed among the cotton bales of a ship bound north, his work as a barber and laborer in Connecticut, and how his old master found him at Litchfield and took all he had in return for his freedom.

title: Negro Slavery Described by a Negro: Being the Narrative of Ashton Warner, a Native of St. Vincent's. With an Appendix, Containing the Testimony of Four Christian Ministers, Recently Returned from the Colonies, on the System of Slavery as It Now Exists
short: Negro Slavery Described by a Negro
author: Ashton Warner
blurb: Ashton Warner, bought free as an infant with his mother by his aunt Daphne Crosbie, tells how at ten he was claimed as a slave of Cane Grove estate in St. Vincent, describes the field gangs' labour, and escapes by sea to London, where he died while the book was in press; four ministers' testimony on colonial slavery follows.

title: Slavery in the United States: A Narrative of the Life and Adventures of Charles Ball, a Black Man
short: The Life and Adventures of Charles Ball
author: Charles Ball
blurb: Charles Ball tells of slavery in Calvert County, Maryland, his sale south in a chained coffle, years on cotton plantations in South Carolina and Georgia, his flight home and service in Commodore Barney's flotilla, his seizure back into slavery in 1830, and his escape by ship from Savannah to Philadelphia.

title: A Narrative of the Adventures and Escape of Moses Roper, from American Slavery
short: The Adventures and Escape of Moses Roper
author: Moses Roper
blurb: Moses Roper, born in Caswell County, North Carolina, to an enslaved mother and her owner, tells of being sold again and again, his many escapes and the tortures that followed them, his final flight by ship to New York in 1834, and his life and lectures in England.

title: A Narrative of Events, Since the First of August, 1834, by James Williams, an Apprenticed Labourer in Jamaica
short: A Narrative of Events, Since the First of August, 1834
author: James Williams
blurb: James Williams, about eighteen, an apprentice at Penshurst in St. Ann's parish, Jamaica, tells of the floggings, the treadmill and the chains of the workhouse he suffered under the new law after August 1834.

title: Poems by a Slave in the Island of Cuba, Recently Liberated; Translated from the Spanish, by R. R. Madden, M.D., with the History of the Early Life of the Negro Poet, Written by Himself; to Which Are Prefixed Two Pieces Descriptive of Cuban Slavery and the Slave-Traffic, by R. R. M.
short: Poems by a Slave in the Island of Cuba
author: Juan Francisco Manzano
blurb: Juan Francisco Manzano tells of his childhood as a favoured house slave in Cuba, the punishments of his youth and his escape on horseback one night; with his poems, translated by R. R. Madden, and Madden's own poems and papers on Cuban slavery and the slave trade.

title: Incidents Connected with the Life of Selim Aga, a Native of Central Africa
short: Incidents Connected with the Life of Selim Aga
author: Selim Aga
blurb: Selim Aga describes his home valley of Tegla, between Durfur and Abyssinia, and tells how he was kidnapped as a boy, sold from master to master through Kordofan, Dongola and Cairo, and brought by a British gentleman by way of Malta and Italy to England; with poems of his own.

title: Narratives of the Sufferings of Lewis and Milton Clarke, Sons of a Soldier of the Revolution, During a Captivity of More Than Twenty Years Among the Slaveholders of Kentucky, One of the So Called Christian States of North America
short: Narratives of Lewis and Milton Clarke
author: Lewis and Milton Clarke
blurb: Lewis Clarke, born in 1815 in Madison County, Kentucky, tells of his mistress Mrs. Banton's cruelties, his escape to Canada and his return to bring out his brother Cyrus; his brother Milton tells of his escape to Oberlin, his seizure by Kentucky kidnappers in Ohio and his rescue, with an appendix of questions and answers on slavery.

title: The Life of Josiah Henson, Formerly a Slave, Now an Inhabitant of Canada, as Narrated by Himself
author: Josiah Henson
with: written down by Samuel A. Eliot
blurb: Josiah Henson tells of his boyhood in Charles County, Maryland, leading his master's slaves to Kentucky, being cheated of the freedom he had paid for and taken to New Orleans to be sold, his escape with his family to Canada in 1830, and the settlement at Dawn.

title: A Narrative of the Life and Travels of Mrs. Nancy Prince
short: The Life and Travels of Mrs. Nancy Prince
author: Nancy Prince
blurb: Nancy Prince, born in Newburyport, Massachusetts, in 1799, tells of her hard early years, nine years in St. Petersburg, where she was presented to the Emperor Alexander and lived through the flood of 1824, her two voyages to Jamaica after emancipation, and her return by way of Key West and New Orleans.

title: Narrative of the Life of Henry Box Brown, Written by Himself
short: Narrative of the Life of Henry Box Brown
author: Henry Box Brown
blurb: Henry Brown tells of his boyhood in slavery in Louisa County, Virginia, his years in a Richmond tobacco factory, the sale of his wife and children, and how he had himself nailed in a box and sent by express to Philadelphia.

title: Biography of Mahommah G. Baquaqua, a Native of Zoogoo, in the Interior of Africa
author: Mahommah Gardo Baquaqua
blurb: Samuel Moore sets down from Mahommah Baquaqua's own words an account of his home city of Zoogoo, in the interior of Africa, his capture and the slave ship to Pernambuco, slavery in Brazil, his escape at New York, his conversion in Haiti and his schooling at McGrawville.

title: Slave Life in Georgia: A Narrative of the Life, Sufferings, and Escape of John Brown, a Fugitive Slave, Now in England
author: John Brown
blurb: John Brown, called Fed in slavery, tells of his sale from Virginia to Georgia, the experiments Dr. Hamilton made on his body, his attempts to escape, and his flight north and on to England.

title: Autobiography of a Fugitive Negro: His Anti-Slavery Labours in the United States, Canada, & England
author: Samuel Ringgold Ward
blurb: Samuel Ringgold Ward, carried out of slavery in Maryland as a child, tells of his family, his years as an abolitionist lecturer and pastor in New York, his flight to Canada after the Jerry rescue at Syracuse in 1851, and his lecturing in England, Scotland, Ireland and Wales.

title: The Life of John Thompson, a Fugitive Slave; Containing His History of 25 Years in Bondage, and His Providential Escape
author: John Thompson
blurb: John Thompson, born in slavery in Maryland in 1812, tells of the sale of his elder sister, Methodist preaching among the slaves, his escape to Philadelphia, and how, with slave hunters about, he shipped from New Bedford as steward of a whaler bound for the Indian Ocean.

title: The Rev. J. W. Loguen, as a Slave and as a Freeman. A Narrative of Real Life
short: The Rev. J. W. Loguen, as a Slave and as a Freeman
author: Jermain Wesley Loguen
blurb: The story of Jermain Loguen, son of the Tennessee slaveholder David Logue and the enslaved Cherry, told in the third person: his boyhood in slavery, his escape to Canada, his schooling and ministry in New York, and his work on the Underground Railroad at Syracuse, with his reply to a letter from Mrs. Logue.

title: An Autobiography. Bond and Free: or, Yearnings for Freedom, from My Green Brier House. Being the Story of My Life in Bondage, and My Life in Freedom
author: Israel Campbell
blurb: Israel Campbell tells of slavery in Kentucky, Mississippi and Tennessee, preaching while still a slave, his escape to Canada, and his life there as a free man and Baptist minister.

title: A True Tale of Slavery
author: John S. Jacobs
blurb: Harriet Jacobs's brother John tells of slavery in Edenton, North Carolina, of gaol after his sister's escape, of his own escape in New York from his master, a member of Congress, of a whaling voyage and of the Fugitive Slave Law.

title: Louisa Picquet, the Octoroon: or Inside Views of Southern Domestic Life
author: Louisa Picquet
blurb: In answers to Hiram Mattison's questions, Louisa Picquet tells how, not yet fourteen, she was sold at Mobile to a New Orleans man and freed at his death; Mattison follows her efforts to buy her mother out of slavery in Texas.

title: The Experience of Thomas H. Jones, Who Was a Slave for Forty-Three Years
short: The Experience of Thomas H. Jones
author: Thomas H. Jones
blurb: Thomas H. Jones tells of his boyhood in Hanover County, North Carolina, learning to read in secret in a Wilmington store, the loss of his first wife and children, and his escape north in 1849, stowed in a brig's hold.

title: Life of James Mars, a Slave Born and Sold in Connecticut
author: James Mars
blurb: James Mars tells how his family hid in Norfolk, Connecticut, from the minister who owned them and meant to take them South, how he was sold at eight to a farmer named Munger, and how his slavery ended in 1815.

title: Life Among the Lowly, Numbers I and III: The Recollections of Madison Hemings and Israel Jefferson
short: Life Among the Lowly: Hemings and Jefferson
author: Madison Hemings and Israel Jefferson
blurb: Two men born enslaved at Monticello tell their lives to an Ohio newspaper in 1873: Madison Hemings says that Thomas Jefferson was his father and Sally Hemings his mother, and Israel Jefferson, sold after Jefferson's death, tells of buying his freedom and confirms Hemings's account.

title: The Autobiography of Nicholas Said; a Native of Bornou, Eastern Soudan, Central Africa
author: Nicholas Said
blurb: Nicholas Said, son of a Bornou general, tells of his capture by Kindill (Tuareg) raiders as a boy, his sale across the Sahara to Tripoli, a pilgrimage to Mecca, slavery in Constantinople, his years with Russian princes, and his travels to the West Indies and America, where he taught school in the South.

title: My Life in the South
author: Jacob Stroyer
blurb: Jacob Stroyer, whose father was brought from Sierra Leone as a boy, describes slavery on the Singleton plantations of South Carolina, his work in the stables, the slaves' beliefs about witches and their ways of finding thieves, runaways and slave hunters, and his labor on the Confederate works at Fort Sumter during the Civil War.

title: Twenty-Eight Years a Slave, or The Story of My Life in Three Continents
author: Thomas L. Johnson
blurb: Thomas L. Johnson tells of his twenty-eight years as a slave in Virginia, freedom at the fall of Richmond, his ministry in Chicago and Denver, his studies at Spurgeon's Pastors' College in London, mission work at Victoria in the Cameroons, and his later years as an evangelist in Britain, with letters and press reports.

title: The Narrative of Bethany Veney, a Slave Woman
author: Bethany Veney
blurb: Bethany Veney tells of slavery in Page County, Virginia, her husband Jerry's sale south, how she kept herself from being sold at Richmond, her purchase by G. J. Adams, and her free life in Worcester, Massachusetts.

title: The House of Bondage, or Charlotte Brooks and Other Slaves
author: Octavia V. Rogers Albert
blurb: Octavia Albert sets down her conversations in Louisiana with Charlotte Brooks, sold south from Virginia to a sugar plantation, and with other men and women once enslaved, who tell of cruel masters, sales and escapes, the war, and the years after freedom.

title: From Slave Cabin to the Pulpit. The Autobiography of Rev. Peter Randolph: The Southern Question Illustrated and Sketches of Slave Life
short: From Slave Cabin to the Pulpit
author: Peter Randolph
blurb: Peter Randolph tells of slavery on Carter H. Edloe's plantation in Prince George County, Virginia, the freeing of Edloe's slaves by his will and their coming to Boston in 1847, and his work as a minister in Boston and in Richmond after the war; his Sketches of Slave Life of 1855 follow.

title: Reminiscences of My Life in Camp with the 33d United States Colored Troops, Late 1st S. C. Volunteers
short: Reminiscences of My Life in Camp
author: Susie King Taylor
blurb: Susie King Taylor, born enslaved in Liberty County, Georgia, and taught to read in secret in Savannah, recalls the war years with the 1st South Carolina Volunteers (the 33d U. S. Colored Troops) as laundress, nurse and teacher, and her later life in Boston and a visit to Louisiana.

title: The Life and Adventures of Nat Love, Better Known in the Cattle Country as "Deadwood Dick": A True History of Slavery Days, Life on the Great Cattle Ranges and on the Plains of the "Wild and Woolly" West, Based on Facts, and Personal Experiences of the Author
short: The Life and Adventures of Nat Love
author: Nat Love
blurb: Born enslaved in Davidson County, Tennessee, in 1854, Nat Love tells of going west as a cowboy, winning the name "Deadwood Dick" at a roping contest in Deadwood, his capture by Indians, and his years as a Pullman porter.

title: Autobiography of Omar ibn Said, Slave in North Carolina, 1831
author: Omar ibn Said
blurb: Omar ibn Said, a Fula scholar from Futa Toro enslaved in North Carolina, writes in Arabic in 1831 of his studies, his capture and sale at Charleston, his jailing at Fayetteville and his life with James Owen, after the Koran passages he remembered; the editor's introduction gathers what else was known of him.

title: A Narrative of Some Remarkable Incidents in the Life of Solomon Bayley, Formerly a Slave, in the State of Delaware, North America
short: Remarkable Incidents in the Life of Solomon Bayley
author: Solomon Bayley
blurb: Solomon Bayley, carried as a slave from Delaware into Virginia, tells of his escape back across the Chesapeake, buying his own freedom, his wife's and his son's, and his conversion, and in letters to Robert Hurnard, who published the book in England, gives accounts of his mother, whose mother was brought from Guinea, and of the deaths of his two daughters.

title: Chains and Freedom: or, The Life and Adventures of Peter Wheeler, a Colored Man Yet Living
author: Peter Wheeler
with: written down by Charles Edwards Lester
blurb: Peter Wheeler, born at Little Egg Harbour, New Jersey, and freed by his old master's will but stolen and sold, tells Charles Edwards Lester of his years under the cruel Gideon Morehouse in Cayuga County, New York, his escape to sea and voyages to the West Indies, Bristol and Gibraltar, the death of his betrothed Solena, and his conversion, with Lester's abolitionist notes.

title: The Life and Sufferings of Leonard Black, a Fugitive from Slavery
short: The Life and Sufferings of Leonard Black
author: Leonard Black
blurb: Leonard Black, enslaved in Maryland, tells of the beatings he suffered as a boy placed with the Bradfords and Mr. Gardner, his flight north to Boston in search of his escaped brothers, his years in Providence with President Wayland, and his call to preach to a Baptist church on Nantucket, and closes with an argument against slavery.

title: Narrative of Henry Watson, a Fugitive Slave
author: Henry Watson
blurb: Henry Watson, born near Fredericksburg, Virginia, about 1813, tells of being sold at auction in Richmond and marched in a drove to Natchez, his years under the McNeill brothers near Vicksburg and in a Vicksburg coffee-house, and his escape by ship to Boston and on to England, with an appendix of extracts on the slave laws and two poems.

title: Struggles for Freedom; or the Life of James Watkins, Formerly a Slave in Maryland, U.S.; in Which Is Detailed a Graphic Account of His Extraordinary Escape from Slavery, Notices of the Fugitive Slave Law, the Sentiments of American Divines on the Subject of Slavery, etc., etc.
author: James Watkins
blurb: James Watkins tells of his childhood and youth as a slave on Abraham Ensor's plantation in Baltimore County, Maryland, his conversion, his two escapes and his years at Hartford, Connecticut, his flight to England after the Fugitive Slave Law of 1850 and his lecturing there, followed by extracts, letters, speeches and poems against slavery and a list of the meetings he held.

title: A North-Side View of Slavery. The Refugee: or the Narratives of Fugitive Slaves in Canada. Related by Themselves, with an Account of the History and Condition of the Colored Population of Upper Canada
author: Benjamin Drew (comp.)
blurb: Benjamin Drew set down in 1855 the narratives of more than a hundred fugitive slaves living in Canada West, at St. Catharines, Toronto, Chatham, Buxton, Windsor and other towns and settlements, among them Harriet Tubman, who tell of their slavery, their escapes and their lives in freedom.

title: A Narrative of Events of the Life of J. H. Banks, an Escaped Slave, from the Cotton State, Alabama, in America
short: The Life of J. H. Banks
author: J. H. Banks
with: written by J. W. C. Pennington
blurb: J. H. Banks, born a slave in Rockingham County, Virginia, tells of his family and the selling of his sisters, his sale at Richmond to an Alabama cotton planter, his fight with the overseer, his flight north, his seven months in the Smithland gaol in Kentucky and his escapes from it and other gaols, until he reached Illinois and, in 1861, Liverpool.

title: The Story of the Life of John Anderson, the Fugitive Slave
short: The Story of the Life of John Anderson
author: John Anderson
blurb: The story of John Anderson, a slave in Missouri who, escaping north in September 1853, fatally wounded Seneca T. P. Diggs, a slaveholder who tried to stop him, reached Canada, and was claimed for extradition in 1860: the court proceedings at Toronto and in London, the meetings held for him, his discharge, his schooling at Corby and his farewell from England for Liberia.

title: Slave Life in Virginia and Kentucky; or, Fifty Years of Slavery in the Southern States of America
short: Slave Life in Virginia and Kentucky
author: Francis Fedric
blurb: Francis Fedric, taken from Fauquier County, Virginia, to a plantation in Mason County, Kentucky, at about fourteen, describes the feeding and punishment of slaves, their weddings, corn songs and parties, the sale of slaves to pay his young master's gambling debts, his flight to a swamp cavern and the 107 lashes that followed, and his escape to Canada and England.

title: Narratives of Colored Americans
author: A. Mott and M. S. Wood (comp.)
blurb: Eighty-one short narratives, anecdotes and poems printed for Colored Americans by the trustees of Lindley Murray’s estate: lives of Phillis Wheatley, Benjamin Banneker, Paul Cuffee, Sojourner Truth, Gustavus Vassa, Lott Carey and Katy Ferguson, and stories of faith, kindness and escape from slavery in America and Africa.

title: Fifty Years of Slavery in the United States of America
author: Harry Smith
blurb: The life of Harry Smith, born a slave in Nelson County, Kentucky, told of him in the third person: his masters the Salones, the patrollers, hunts, cock fights and slave sales, the guerrillas of the Civil War, his freedom, and his later life in Indiana and Michigan, with a sketch of his wife, Hagar.

title: Life of Isaac Mason as a Slave
short: Life of Isaac Mason as a Slave
author: Isaac Mason
blurb: Isaac Mason, born in 1822 in Kent County, Maryland, tells of being hired out and whipped as a boy, his escape north through Delaware into Pennsylvania, his flight from the Fugitive Slave Law to Worcester, Massachusetts, and for a time to Canada, and a voyage to Haiti under James Redpath's emigration scheme.

title: The New Man: Twenty-Nine Years a Slave, Twenty-Nine Years a Free Man
author: H. C. Bruce
blurb: H. C. Bruce, born a slave in Prince Edward County, Virginia, in 1836, recalls his years in Virginia, the cotton fields of Mississippi and the tobacco factories and farms of Missouri, his flight to Kansas in 1864 with the woman he married, and his life as a freedman in business, Kansas politics and the Pension Office at Washington, with essays on the progress of the Colored people.

title: Recollections of Slavery Times
author: Allen Parker
blurb: Allen Parker recalls his childhood and youth as a slave near Chowan, North Carolina: the cabins, food and clothing of the slaves, their courtships and marriages, coon hunting and merry-making, punishments, and his escape in 1862 to a Union gunboat, his year in the navy and his life afterwards in the North.

title: The Story of My Life and Work
short: The Story of My Life and Work
author: Booker T. Washington
blurb: Booker T. Washington’s autobiography of 1900, sold by subscription: his birth in slavery in Franklin County, Virginia, his boyhood in the salt furnaces and coal mines of West Virginia, Hampton, the building of Tuskegee, the Atlanta Exposition address, his Harvard degree, his vacation in Europe and President McKinley’s visit to Tuskegee.

title: Shadow and Light: An Autobiography, with Reminiscences of the Last and Present Century
author: Mifflin Wistar Gibbs
blurb: Mifflin Wistar Gibbs, born free in Philadelphia in 1823, tells of the Underground Railroad and lecturing with Frederick Douglass, merchant life in Gold Rush San Francisco, trade and a coal company in British Columbia, his years as a lawyer, municipal judge and Republican officeholder in Arkansas, and his service as United States consul at Tamatave, Madagascar.

title: The Heir of Slaves: An Autobiography
author: William Pickens
blurb: William Pickens tells of his boyhood in South Carolina, his family's move to an Arkansas plantation and their escape from its debts, his schooling at Argenta, across the river from Little Rock, while he worked at a stave factory and a sawmill, and his studies at Talladega College and at Yale, where he won the Ten Eyck prize in oratory, before returning to teach at Talladega.

title: Reminiscences of School Life, and Hints on Teaching
author: Fanny Jackson Coppin
blurb: Fanny Jackson Coppin, whose aunt bought her freedom, tells of her schooling, her studies at Oberlin College and her work at the Institute for Colored Youth in Philadelphia, sets out her methods of teaching reading, grammar, geography and arithmetic, and describes her visits to England and South Africa, followed by sketches of the Institute's teachers and graduates.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Alabama Narratives
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews, Aarons to Young, with formerly enslaved people in Alabama, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, many in Mobile and others around Opelika, Livingston, Eufaula and Uniontown, with spirituals and the Rev. W.E. Northcross's autobiography of 1897.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Arkansas Narratives, Part 1
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews, Abbott to Byrd, with formerly enslaved people in Arkansas and some of their children, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, many in Pine Bluff and Little Rock and others in the Delta towns from Brinkley to Helena.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Arkansas Narratives, Part 2
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews, Cannon to Fritz, with formerly enslaved people in Arkansas and some of their children, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, most in Pine Bluff, Little Rock and El Dorado, with slavery-time songs, superstitions and customs.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Arkansas Narratives, Part 3
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews, Gadson to Isom, with formerly enslaved people in Arkansas and some of their children, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, most in Pine Bluff, Little Rock and the farm towns around Brinkley and Biscoe.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Arkansas Narratives, Part 4
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews, Jackson to Lynch, with formerly enslaved people in Arkansas and some of their children, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, most in Pine Bluff and Little Rock, among them a bill of sale of 1840 and memories of Reconstruction officeholders.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Arkansas Narratives, Part 5
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews, McClendon to Prayer, with formerly enslaved people in Arkansas and some of their children, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, many in Pine Bluff and the rest mostly in Little Rock and the towns around Brinkley.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Arkansas Narratives, Part 6
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews, Quinn to Tuttle, with formerly enslaved people in Arkansas and some of their children, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, most in Pine Bluff, Little Rock and Brinkley, with folklore from Texarkana and El Dorado.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Arkansas Narratives, Part 7
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews, Vaden to Young, with formerly enslaved people in Arkansas and some of their children, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, most in Pine Bluff and Little Rock, with a marriage license and an 1874 church programme kept by Julia A. White.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Florida Narratives
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews with formerly enslaved people in Florida, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, many by its Negro Writers' Unit, in Jacksonville, Tampa, Miami and smaller towns across the state.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Georgia Narratives, Part 1
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews, Adams to Furr, with formerly enslaved people in Georgia, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project in Athens, Augusta, Atlanta, Columbus, Macon and elsewhere, with folklore and conjure tales.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Georgia Narratives, Part 2
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews, Garey to Jones, with formerly enslaved people in Georgia, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, many in Athens and Augusta and others in Columbus, Macon and Washington-Wilkes, with spirituals and folk beliefs.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Georgia Narratives, Part 3
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews, Kendricks to Styles, with formerly enslaved people in Georgia, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, many in Athens and Augusta and others in Columbus, Macon and Milledgeville.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Georgia Narratives, Part 4
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews, Telfair to Young, with formerly enslaved people in Georgia, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, mostly in Augusta and Athens, followed by combined interviews, Atlanta folklore and Richmond County compilations on conjuration, folk remedies and slavery.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Indiana Narratives
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews with formerly enslaved people and their children in Indiana, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project in Indianapolis, Evansville, Gary, New Albany and other towns, most of them recalling slavery in Kentucky.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Kansas Narratives
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Three interviews with formerly enslaved people living in Kansas, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project in Ottawa and Hutchinson, recalling slavery in Tennessee, Missouri and Arkansas, the Civil War and the move to Kansas.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Kentucky Narratives
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews with formerly enslaved people in Kentucky, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, followed by county reports on local slavery, tales, songs, a bill of sale and a will.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Maryland Narratives
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Twenty-two interviews with formerly enslaved people in Maryland, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, most in Baltimore, telling of plantation work, sales, escapes, the Civil War and freedom.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Mississippi Narratives
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Twenty-six interviews with formerly enslaved people in Mississippi, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, among them James Lucas, who was once owned by Jefferson Davis.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Missouri Narratives
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews with formerly enslaved people in Missouri, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project in St. Louis, Cape Girardeau, Fredericktown, Farmington, Hannibal and smaller towns, with the songs, riddles and rhymes they remembered.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, North Carolina Narratives, Part 1
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Eighty-nine interviews, Adams to Hunter, with formerly enslaved people in North Carolina, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, mostly around Raleigh, Durham, Wilmington and Asheville.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, North Carolina Narratives, Part 2
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Eighty-eight interviews, Jackson to Yellerday, with formerly enslaved people in North Carolina, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, many of them in and around Raleigh, with others from Wilmington, Durham, Asheville and Rockingham County.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Ohio Narratives
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Interviews with formerly enslaved people in Ohio, recorded in 1937 by the Federal Writers' Project in Cincinnati, Youngstown, Toledo, Steubenville and other towns, recalling slavery from Virginia and Kentucky to Georgia, Alabama and Louisiana.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Oklahoma Narratives
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Seventy-five interviews with formerly enslaved people in Oklahoma, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project in Oklahoma City, Tulsa, Fort Gibson and smaller towns, among them people once owned by Creek, Cherokee and Chickasaw masters.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, South Carolina Narratives, Part 1
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Eighty-nine interviews, Abrams to Durant, with formerly enslaved people in South Carolina, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, from Winnsboro, Union and Newberry to Marion and the Georgetown coast.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, South Carolina Narratives, Part 2
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Eighty-five interviews, Eddington to Hunter, with formerly enslaved people in South Carolina, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, from Spartanburg, Newberry and Winnsboro to Columbia, Marion, Charleston and the Georgetown coast.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, South Carolina Narratives, Part 3
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Eighty-two interviews, Jackson to Quattlebaum, with formerly enslaved people in South Carolina, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project in Union, Newberry, Winnsboro, Spartanburg, Columbia and Charleston, on Edisto Island and in Beaufort County.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, South Carolina Narratives, Part 4
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Eighty-four interviews and songs, Raines to Young, with formerly enslaved people in South Carolina, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, from Winnsboro, Newberry, Union and Spartanburg to Marion, Columbia and the Georgetown coast.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Tennessee Narratives
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Twenty-six interviews with formerly enslaved people in Tennessee, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, most in Nashville and a few in Knoxville, with spirituals and memories of freedom.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Texas Narratives, Part 1
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Eighty-seven interviews, Adams to Duhon, with formerly enslaved people in Texas, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, recalling slavery across the South, the Civil War and freedom in Texas.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Texas Narratives, Part 2
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Seventy-three interviews, Easter to King, with formerly enslaved people in Texas, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, recalling slavery across the South, the Civil War and freedom in Texas.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Texas Narratives, Part 3
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Seventy-five interviews, Lewis to Ryles, with formerly enslaved people in Texas, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, recalling slavery across the South, the Civil War and freedom in Texas.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Texas Narratives, Part 4
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Seventy interviews, Sanco to Young, with formerly enslaved people in Texas, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project, recalling slavery across the South, the Civil War and freedom in Texas.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Virginia Narratives
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: Fourteen interviews with formerly enslaved people in Virginia, recorded 1936–38 by the Federal Writers' Project in Petersburg, Norfolk, Portsmouth and the Tidewater, with songs, folk beliefs and wartime memories.

title: Slave Narratives: A Folk History of Slavery in the United States from Interviews with Former Slaves, Administrative Files: Selected Records Bearing on the History of the Slave Narratives
author: Federal Writers' Project
blurb: The project's own papers on the slave narratives: B.A. Botkin's 1941 introduction to the collection, and nine memoranda and instructions of 1937 from the Federal Writers' Project's Washington office, among them John A. Lomax's questionnaire for interviewers and Sterling A. Brown's notes on dialect.

title: Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species, Humbly Submitted to the Inhabitants of Great-Britain
short: Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil of Slavery
author: Ottobah Cugoano
blurb: Ottobah Cugoano, a Fante man kidnapped as a boy, enslaved in Grenada and freed in England, tells of his capture and argues from scripture, law and history that the slave trade and slavery are robbery and murder, that the enslaved may rightly resist, and that Britain should abolish both at once.

title: The Past and the Present Condition, and the Destiny, of the Colored Race: A Discourse Delivered at the Fifteenth Anniversary of the Female Benevolent Society of Troy, N.Y., Feb. 14, 1848
short: The Destiny of the Colored Race
author: Henry Highland Garnet
blurb: Henry Highland Garnet’s 1848 discourse at Troy, New York, surveying the African past, the present condition of the colored race under slavery and prejudice, and its destiny in America.

title: The Freedman's Story: In Two Parts
author: William Parker
blurb: William Parker tells of his boyhood in Maryland, his escape to Pennsylvania, and the fight at his house near Christiana in 1851 in which a slaveholder hunting fugitives was killed; his editor adds an account of the riot.

title: Life and Public Services of Martin R. Delany, Sub-Assistant Commissioner Bureau Relief of Refugees, Freedmen, and of Abandoned Lands, and Late Major 104th U.S. Colored Troops
short: Life and Public Services of Martin R. Delany
author: Frank A. Rollin
blurb: Frances Rollin’s life of Martin R. Delany: physician, editor, emigrationist, Niger Valley explorer, first Black major in the Union army, Freedmen’s Bureau agent; with his political writings.

title: Civil Rights. The Outrage of the Supreme Court of the United States upon the Black Man. Reviewed in a Reply to the New York "Voice," the Great Temperance Paper of the United States
short: Civil Rights: The Outrage of the Supreme Court
author: Henry McNeal Turner
blurb: Bishop Henry McNeal Turner answers a reader's question put to him by the New York Voice about the Supreme Court's Civil Rights decisions of 1883, quoting the Civil Rights Act of 1875 and Justice Harlan's dissent, followed by his address of 1884 to the ministers and members of his episcopal district.

title: The Barbarous Decision of the United States Supreme Court Declaring the Civil Rights Act Unconstitutional and Disrobing the Colored Race of All Civil Protection. The Most Cruel and Inhuman Verdict Against a Loyal People in the History of the World. Also the Powerful Speeches of Hon. Frederick Douglass and Col. Robert G. Ingersoll, Jurist and Famous Orator
author: Henry McNeal Turner (comp.)
blurb: Bishop H. M. Turner prints the Civil Rights Act of 1875, the Supreme Court's 1883 decision striking it down with Justice Harlan's dissent, and the protest speeches of Frederick Douglass and Robert G. Ingersoll.

title: A Review of Hoffman's Race Traits and Tendencies of the American Negro
short: A Review of Hoffman's Race Traits
author: Kelly Miller
blurb: Kelly Miller answers, chapter by chapter, the insurance statistician Frederick Hoffman’s claim that the American Negro was dying out through inborn race traits, using Hoffman’s own figures.

title: Right on the Scaffold, or The Martyrs of 1822
author: Archibald H. Grimké
blurb: Archibald Grimké’s account of Denmark Vesey’s planned slave rising in Charleston in 1822, its betrayal, the trials, and the hanging of Vesey and his companions.

title: John Brown
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
blurb: Du Bois’s life of John Brown, told from the side of the Black Americans he lived and worked among: Kansas, the great plan, Harper’s Ferry, the trial and its legacy.

title: The Crisis: A Record of the Darker Races, Volume One, Number One, November 1910
author: W. E. B. Du Bois (ed.)
blurb: The first number of the NAACP’s monthly, edited by W. E. B. Du Bois: news along the color line, opinion, editorials, Moorfield Storey on Brownsville, a reading list, advertisements.

title: The Crisis: A Record of the Darker Races, Volume One, Number Three, January 1911
author: W. E. B. Du Bois (ed.)
blurb: The third number of the NAACP’s monthly, edited by W. E. B. Du Bois: news along the color line, opinion on the appeal to Europe and the Baltimore ghetto, Du Bois’s “A Winter Pilgrimage,” editorials, Jane Addams on social control, a poem by Leslie Pinckney Hill, a study of colored women’s work in Chicago, the year-by-year count of lynchings, a reading list, advertisements.

title: The Negro and the Nation
author: Hubert H. Harrison
blurb: Hubert Harrison’s first book: six articles from the socialist and radical press, 1912–1917, on the Black man’s burden, socialism and the Negro, conservatism, and the newspapers’ treatment of the race.

title: When Africa Awakes: The "Inside Story" of the Stirrings and Strivings of the New Negro in the Western World
author: Hubert H. Harrison
blurb: Hubert Harrison’s editorials and articles of 1917–1920 on the Liberty League, lynching, the war, the New Negro in politics, race-first radicalism, Africa and the colonial world, with book reviews.

title: An Address to the Negroes in the State of New-York
short: An Address to the Negroes in the State of New-York
author: Jupiter Hammon
blurb: Jupiter Hammon, past seventy and enslaved on Long Island, urges his fellow Black New Yorkers to obedience, honesty and religion, says he hopes the young may be freed, and calls on the free to live so as to help those still in bondage.

title: A Narrative of the Proceedings of the Black People, During the Late Awful Calamity in Philadelphia, in the Year 1793: And a Refutation of Some Censures, Thrown upon Them in Some Late Publications
short: A Narrative of the Proceedings of the Black People
author: Absalom Jones and Richard Allen
blurb: Absalom Jones and Richard Allen tell how they and other Black Philadelphians nursed the sick, bled patients and buried the dead in the yellow fever epidemic of 1793, answer Mathew Carey's charge that Black nurses extorted money, and add addresses against slavery and to the people of colour.

title: Walker's Appeal, with a Brief Sketch of His Life; and also Garnet's Address to the Slaves of the United States of America
author: David Walker
blurb: David Walker's 1829 Appeal urges the colored citizens of the world to resist slavery; Henry Highland Garnet adds a sketch of Walker's life and his 1843 Address to the Slaves.

title: Essays; Including Biographies and Miscellaneous Pieces, in Prose and Poetry
author: Ann Plato
blurb: Ann Plato, a young member of James W. C. Pennington's church in Hartford who taught school, writes essays on religion, education and conduct, memoirs of four young women of her acquaintance who had died, and poems, among them "The Natives of America" and "To the First of August"; Pennington introduces her.

title: An Address to All the Colored Citizens of the United States
short: An Address to All the Colored Citizens
author: John B. Meachum
blurb: John B. Meachum, born a slave in Virginia and pastor of the African Baptist Church in St. Louis, tells how he bought his own freedom and then his father's, his wife's and his children's, and calls on the free colored people of the United States to unite, to school their children, to take up farming and to keep a day of fasting and prayer, announcing a national convention at Pittsburg in 1847.

title: The Condition, Elevation, Emigration, and Destiny of the Colored People of the United States
short: The Condition of the Colored People
author: Martin Robison Delany
blurb: Martin R. Delany surveys the condition and achievements of free colored Americans, condemns the colonization of Liberia, and argues for emigration to Central and South America and the West Indies.

title: Collected Articles of Frederick Douglass
author: Frederick Douglass
blurb: Two magazine articles by Frederick Douglass: "My Escape from Slavery" (1881), telling how he fled Maryland disguised as a sailor, and "Reconstruction" (1866), urging Congress to enfranchise the freedmen.

title: John Brown: An Address at the Fourteenth Anniversary of Storer College
author: Frederick Douglass
blurb: Frederick Douglass, speaking at Harper's Ferry in 1881, recalls his friendship with John Brown, recounts the 1859 raid, and argues that Brown began the war that ended slavery.

title: Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases
author: Ida B. Wells
blurb: Ida B. Wells's 1892 pamphlet, written after a mob destroyed her Memphis newspaper, examines the charge of rape used to excuse lynching and urges self-help, boycott and emigration.

title: A Voice from the South, by a Black Woman of the South
author: Anna Julia Cooper
blurb: Anna Julia Cooper's essays in two parts: on Black women's place in the progress of the race, their higher education and their status in America, then on the race problem, the Negro as drawn in American literature, what the race is worth, and the gain from a belief.

title: The Reason Why the Colored American Is Not in the World's Columbian Exposition: The Afro-American's Contribution to Columbian Literature
author: Ida B. Wells, Frederick Douglass, I. Garland Penn and F. L. Barnett
blurb: The pamphlet handed out at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, with prefaces in French and German: Frederick Douglass introduces it, Ida B. Wells writes on discriminatory laws, the convict lease system and lynching, I. Garland Penn on progress since emancipation, and F. L. Barnett on the exclusion of Black Americans from the Exposition.

title: The Work of the Afro-American Woman
short: The Work of the Afro-American Woman
author: Mrs. N. F. (Gertrude Bustill) Mossell
blurb: Gertrude Mossell surveys the work of Black American women in teaching, literature, journalism and the professions, with Ida B. Wells’s campaign against lynching, poems by Wheatley, Harper and others, essays on home and on caste in colored colleges, and her own verse.

title: Why Is the Negro Lynched? (“The Lesson of the Hour”)
author: Frederick Douglass
blurb: Frederick Douglass’s 1894 address “The Lesson of the Hour,” reprinted in England after his death: he answers the charge of assaults on white women used to excuse lynching in the South, argues that the persecution aims at taking away the Negro’s vote, and rejects schemes of colonization.

title: The Red Record: Tabulated Statistics and Alleged Causes of Lynching in the United States
author: Ida B. Wells
blurb: Ida B. Wells's 1895 record of lynchings in the United States, drawn from the Chicago Tribune's figures for 1892–1894, with case histories, her dispute with Frances Willard, and proposed remedies.

title: The Conservation of Races
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
blurb: Du Bois's 1897 paper for the American Negro Academy argues that each race has a message for humanity and that Black Americans should keep their race identity.

title: Civilization the Primal Need of the Race, and The Attitude of the American Mind Toward the Negro Intellect
short: Civilization the Primal Need of the Race
author: Alexander Crummell
blurb: Alexander Crummell’s two 1897 addresses as president of the American Negro Academy, arguing that the race’s first need is civilization, through literature, art and philosophy, and that the American mind has long sought to stamp out the Negro intellect.

title: The Future of the American Negro
short: The Future of the American Negro
author: Booker T. Washington
blurb: Booker T. Washington argues that industrial education is the way forward for Black Americans in the South, describing Tuskegee's work and discussing politics, the franchise and lynching.

title: Lynch Law in Georgia: A Six-Weeks’ Record in the Center of Southern Civilization, as Faithfully Chronicled by the “Atlanta Journal” and the “Atlanta Constitution”; Also the Full Report of Louis P. Le Vin, the Chicago Detective Sent to Investigate the Burning of Samuel Hose, the Torture and Hanging of Elijah Strickland, the Colored Preacher, and the Lynching of Nine Men for Alleged Arson
author: Ida B. Wells
blurb: Ida B. Wells-Barnett’s 1899 pamphlet on twelve lynchings in Georgia in six weeks, among them the burning of Samuel Hose and the hanging of the preacher Elijah Strickland, set out from the Atlanta papers’ own accounts and the report of Louis P. Le Vin, a Chicago detective sent to find the facts.

title: Mob Rule in New Orleans: Robert Charles and His Fight to Death, the Story of His Life, Burning Human Beings Alive, Other Lynching Statistics
author: Ida B. Wells
blurb: Ida B. Wells's account of the New Orleans riot of July 1900, when Robert Charles fought off a police assault and mobs attacked Black residents, with lynching statistics.

title: Defense of the Negro Race—Charges Answered. Speech of Hon. George H. White, of North Carolina, in the House of Representatives, January 29, 1901
author: George H. White
blurb: In his last speech to the House, on January 29, 1901, the North Carolina congressman answers the attacks on his race, pleads for the depositors of the Freedman's Savings and Trust Company, and calls it the Negro's temporary farewell to Congress.

title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
blurb: Du Bois's essays on the color line and double consciousness, the Freedmen's Bureau, Booker T. Washington, the Black Belt, Black faith and education, and the Sorrow Songs.

title: The Negro Problem: A Series of Articles by Representative American Negroes of To-day
author: Booker T. Washington, W. E. B. Du Bois, et al.
blurb: Seven essays on the condition and future of Black Americans: Washington on industrial education, Du Bois's "The Talented Tenth", Chesnutt on disfranchisement, and pieces by Smith, Kealing, Dunbar and Fortune.

title: Masterpieces of Negro Eloquence: The Best Speeches Delivered by the Negro from the Days of Slavery to the Present Time
author: Alice Moore Dunbar (ed.)
blurb: Alice Moore Dunbar's anthology of fifty-one speeches by Black orators from 1818 to 1913, among them Frederick Douglass, Frances Harper, Henry Highland Garnet, Alexander Crummell and Booker T. Washington.

title: Darkwater: Voices from Within the Veil
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
blurb: Du Bois's essays on his own life, white supremacy, Africa and empire, work and wealth, democracy, women and children, alternating with poems, prayers and parables.

title: Self-Determining Haiti
author: James Weldon Johnson
blurb: James Weldon Johnson's four 1920 articles for The Nation report on the American occupation of Haiti, its killings, forced labor and financial control, with the treaty and other documents.

title: The New Negro: An Interpretation
author: Alain Locke (ed.)
blurb: Alain Locke’s anthology of the Harlem Renaissance: essays by Locke, Barnes, Braithwaite, Schomburg, James Weldon Johnson, Du Bois and others, stories by Fisher, Toomer, Hurston and Walrond, poems by Cullen, McKay and Hughes, Richardson’s play Compromise, and folk tales.

title: Aesop's Fables
author: Aesop
blurb: Over three hundred fables in Townsend’s 1867 translation, from the Wolf and the Lamb to the Fox and the Grapes, with his life of the slave storyteller Aesop.

title: An Account of Egypt
author: Herodotus
blurb: Book II of Herodotus’s Histories, the Greek traveller’s account of Egypt in the fifth century BC: the Nile, its gods, animals and customs, and the history of its kings.

title: Oroonoko; or, The Royal Slave
author: Aphra Behn
blurb: Aphra Behn's 1688 tale of Oroonoko, an African prince of Coramantien sold into slavery in Surinam with his beloved Imoinda, and the revolt he leads; with Montague Summers's notes.

title: Some Memoirs of the Life of Job, the Son of Solomon, the High Priest of Boonda in Africa; Who Was a Slave about Two Years in Maryland; and Afterwards Being Brought to England, Was Set Free, and Sent to His Native Land in the Year 1734
short: The Life of Job, the Son of Solomon
author: Thomas Bluett
blurb: Thomas Bluett sets down the story of Job, son of the high priest of Boonda in Futa: his capture on the Gambia in 1730, his slavery in Maryland, his welcome in England, his voyage home, and the customs of his country.

title: A Narrative of the Most Remarkable Particulars in the Life of James Albert Ukawsaw Gronniosaw, an African Prince, as Related by Himself
short: The Life of James Albert Ukawsaw Gronniosaw
author: James Albert Ukawsaw Gronniosaw
blurb: Dictated in old age: a Bornu prince is sold into slavery on the Guinea coast, freed in New York, and lives poor but devout in England.

title: Letters of the Late Ignatius Sancho, an African, to Which Are Prefixed Memoirs of His Life
author: Ignatius Sancho
blurb: Letters of Ignatius Sancho, born on a slave ship and later a London grocer, composer and man of letters, written to friends from 1768 to 1780, with a memoir.

title: The Ruins; or, Meditation on the Revolutions of Empires, and the Law of Nature
author: C. F. Volney
blurb: Volney's 1791 meditation among the ruins of Palmyra on why empires fall, holding that Black Ethiopians first discovered the arts and sciences and founded religion; with The Law of Nature.

title: Antar, a Bedoueen Romance
author: Anonymous
blurb: First part of the Arabian romance of Antar, son of an Arab chief and an enslaved Black woman, who rises by valour and poetry, seeking his cousin Ibla.

title: An Account of Timbuctoo and Housa, Territories in the Interior of Africa, by El Hage Abd Salam Shabeeny; with Notes, Critical and Explanatory; to Which Is Added, Letters Descriptive of Travels through West and South Barbary, and across the Mountains of Atlas; also, Fragments, Notes, and Anecdotes; Specimens of the Arabic Epistolary Style, &c. &c.
short: An Account of Timbuctoo and Housa
author: El Hage Abd Salam Shabeeny
blurb: El Hage Abd Salam Shabeeny, a merchant of Tetuan, describes the caravan road from Fas to Timbuctoo and on to Housa, and life in both, as he knew them about 1787, with James Grey Jackson’s notes, his letters of travel in Morocco, and his essays, anecdotes, vocabularies and letters on African trade, languages, the plague and the death of Mungo Park.

title: The Hour and the Man: An Historical Romance
author: Harriet Martineau
blurb: Harriet Martineau's 1841 novel of Toussaint L'Ouverture, from the 1791 slave rising in Saint Domingo through his rule to his betrayal and death in a French fortress.

title: Travels of an Arab Merchant in Soudan (the Black Kingdoms of Central Africa)
short: Travels of an Arab Merchant in Soudan
author: Mohammed ibn Omar el-Tounsy
blurb: Sheikh Mohammed of Tunis recalls years as a young trader in the Black sultanates of Darfur and Wadai: their courts, wars, slave raids and customs. Abridged from the French.

title: Three Years in Europe; or, Places I Have Seen and People I Have Met
author: William Wells Brown
blurb: William Wells Brown’s letters from his first years abroad, 1849 to 1851: the Paris Peace Congress, with Victor Hugo’s speech and a soirée at de Tocqueville’s, London and the Great Exhibition, Ireland and Scotland, Byron’s grave and Harriet Martineau, fugitive slaves in England, with William Farmer’s memoir of Brown’s life.

title: St. Domingo, Its Revolution and Its Hero, Toussaint Louverture
author: Charles Wyllys Elliott
blurb: An 1855 New York lecture on the life of Toussaint Louverture: slavery in St. Domingo, the revolution, his rule, his betrayal by Napoleon and death in a French prison.

title: A Colored Man Round the World
short: A Colored Man Round the World
author: David F. Dorr
blurb: David F. Dorr, enslaved in New Orleans, describes his three-year tour of 1851–54 with his owner through England, France, Germany, Italy, Constantinople, Greece, Egypt and the Holy Land.

title: Official Report of the Niger Valley Exploring Party
short: Report of the Niger Valley Exploring Party
author: Martin Robison Delany
blurb: Martin Delany's report of his 1859–60 journey to Liberia and the Yoruba country seeking land for African American settlement, with his treaty at Abbeokuta and his British tour.

title: Toussaint L'Ouverture: A Biography and Autobiography
short: Toussaint L'Ouverture: A Biography and Autobiography
author: John R. Beard and Toussaint L'Ouverture
blurb: John R. Beard's life of Toussaint L'Ouverture, from slavery in Saint Domingo through the revolution to his death in the Chateau de Joux, with the memoir Toussaint wrote there for Bonaparte and testimonies by Christophe, Martineau, Wordsworth, Whittier and Wendell Phillips.

title: The Rising Son; or, The Antecedents and Advancement of the Colored Race
author: William Wells Brown
blurb: William Wells Brown's history of the African race: ancient Ethiopia, Egypt and Carthage, Africa and the slave trade, Liberia, Haiti, Jamaica, Black America through the Civil War, and biographies.

title: Froudacity: West Indian Fables by James Anthony Froude, Explained by J. J. Thomas
author: J. J. Thomas
blurb: The Trinidadian schoolmaster J. J. Thomas answers James Anthony Froude's The English in the West Indies point by point, defending Black West Indians and their fitness for self-government.

title: African Letters
author: Henry McNeal Turner
blurb: Bishop Henry McNeal Turner writes home of his voyage in 1891 by way of Madeira and the Canary Islands to Sierra Leone and Liberia, of the African people and churches he met there and of the A. M. E. conference in Liberia, followed by two addresses of welcome made to him at Monrovia.

title: Egyptian Tales, Translated from the Papyri: First Series, IVth to XIIth Dynasty
author: W. M. Flinders Petrie (ed.)
blurb: Four tales from Middle Kingdom papyri: King Khufu and the magicians, the eloquent peasant, the shipwrecked sailor, and the exile Sanehat, translated by Flinders Petrie with his remarks on each.

title: Egyptian Tales, Translated from the Papyri: Second Series, XVIIIth to XIXth Dynasty
author: W. M. Flinders Petrie (ed.)
blurb: Four New Kingdom tales from the papyri: the taking of Joppa, the doomed prince, the two brothers Anpu and Bata, and Setna and the magic book, with Petrie’s remarks.

title: Africa and the American Negro . . . Addresses and Proceedings of the Congress on Africa Held under the Auspices of the Stewart Missionary Foundation for Africa of Gammon Theological Seminary in Connection with the Cotton States and International Exposition, December 13-15, 1895
author: J. W. E. Bowen (ed.)
blurb: The addresses given at the Congress on Africa held at Gammon Theological Seminary, Atlanta, in December 1895, among them papers by Alexander Crummell, Orishatukeh Faduma, Henry McNeal Turner, T. Thomas Fortune and Heli Chatelain on African peoples, religions, missions, slavery and the partition of the continent, and on the American Negro's relation to Africa, with the minutes of the congress.

title: How the Black St. Domingo Legion Saved the Patriot Army in the Siege of Savannah, 1779
short: The Black St. Domingo Legion at Savannah
author: T. G. Steward
blurb: Chaplain T. G. Steward tells how free Black volunteers from Saint-Domingue covered the retreat at Savannah in 1779, among them men who would later lead the Haitian Revolution.

title: Zanzibar Tales, Told by Natives of the East Coast of Africa
author: George W. Bateman (trans.)
blurb: Ten Swahili tales told in Zanzibar, of the monkey and the shark, the clever hare, the gazelle who served Haamdaanee, and the boy hunter, translated by George W. Bateman.

title: Jamaican Song and Story: Annancy Stories, Digging Sings, Ring Tunes, and Dancing Tunes
author: Walter Jekyll (ed.)
blurb: Annancy stories, digging-sings, ring tunes and dancing tunes collected from Black Jamaicans by Walter Jekyll, with his notes on their speech, and essays on their African and English roots.

title: The Black Man, the Father of Civilization, Proven by Biblical History
short: The Black Man, the Father of Civilization
author: James Morris Webb
blurb: An evangelist argues from the Bible that Ham’s descendants founded civilization and Solomon and Jesus were of Black descent; with Pixley ka Isaka Seme’s oration "The Regeneration of Africa".

title: Native Life in South Africa, Before and Since the European War and the Boer Rebellion
author: Sol T. Plaatje
blurb: Sol Plaatje, secretary of the South African Native National Congress, documents the 1913 Natives' Land Act, the evictions it caused, the deputation to London, and the Boer rebellion.

title: West African Folk-Tales
author: W. H. Barker and Cecilia Sinclair
blurb: Thirty-six tales of the Gold Coast, eighteen of them of Anansi the spider, gathered from students of the Government training institution for teachers at Accra, with W. H. Barker’s introduction on the folk-lore of the Gold Coast peoples and how it was changing.

title: My Life and Work
author: Alexander Walters
blurb: Bishop Alexander Walters of the A. M. E. Zion Church, born a slave at Bardstown, Kentucky, tells of his youth, his pastorates from Louisville to San Francisco and New York, his travels in Europe, Egypt, the Holy Land and West Africa, and his work in the Afro-American Council and the Pan-African Conference of 1900, with many of his speeches.

title: Alexander Crummell: An Apostle of Negro Culture
author: William H. Ferris
blurb: William H. Ferris's 1920 tribute to Alexander Crummell, the scholar-priest who studied at Cambridge, worked twenty years in Liberia, and founded the American Negro Academy.

title: Wonderful Ethiopians of the Ancient Cushite Empire, Book I: Nations of the Cushite Empire, Marvelous Facts from Authentic Records
short: Wonderful Ethiopians of the Ancient Cushite Empire
author: Drusilla Dunjee Houston
blurb: Drusilla Dunjee Houston argues that an ancient Cushite empire of Ethiopians was the source of civilization and that its people built the early cultures of Egypt, Arabia, Chaldea, India, Media and Persia; this is Book I of a larger work whose later volumes her preface outlines.

title: Colored Americans in the Wars of 1776 and 1812
author: William C. Nell
blurb: William C. Nell’s state-by-state record of Black soldiers and sailors in the Revolution and the War of 1812, from Crispus Attucks to the free colored battalions at New Orleans.

title: The Colored Patriots of the American Revolution, with Sketches of Several Distinguished Colored Persons: To Which Is Added a Brief Survey of the Condition and Prospects of Colored Americans
short: The Colored Patriots of the American Revolution
author: William C. Nell
blurb: William C. Nell's state-by-state record of Black soldiers and patriots of the Revolution and the War of 1812, with sketches of Crispus Attucks, Phillis Wheatley, James Forten and others, and a survey of colored Americans in his own day.

title: The Black Man: His Antecedents, His Genius, and His Achievements
author: William Wells Brown
blurb: William Wells Brown’s memoir of his life, an essay on the African past, and fifty-seven sketches of Black achievers, from Banneker, Toussaint and Nat Turner to Douglass and Frances Watkins.

title: The Negro in the American Rebellion: His Heroism and His Fidelity
short: The Negro in the American Rebellion
author: William Wells Brown
blurb: William Wells Brown’s record of Black soldiers and sailors from the Revolution and 1812 through slave revolts and the Civil War: Fort Wagner, Port Hudson, Fort Pillow, Olustee, and Petersburg.

title: History of the Negro Race in America from 1619 to 1880, Volume 1
short: History of the Negro Race in America, I
author: George Washington Williams
blurb: Williams's first volume: the unity of mankind, African kingdoms, Sierra Leone and Liberia, slavery in each of the thirteen colonies, Black soldiers in the Revolution, and slavery under the Constitution.

title: History of the Negro Race in America from 1619 to 1880, Volume 2
short: History of the Negro Race in America, II
author: George Washington Williams
blurb: Williams's second volume, 1800 to 1880: the slavery debates, the anti-slavery movement, insurrections, Black soldiers and sailors, the Civil War and emancipation, Reconstruction, and Black churches and leaders after freedom.

title: Black and White: Land, Labor, and Politics in the South
author: T. Thomas Fortune
blurb: Journalist T. Thomas Fortune examines land, labor and politics in the post-Reconstruction South, arguing that its troubles are those of capital and labor, rooted in land monopoly, with Senate testimony.

title: The Black Phalanx: A History of the Negro Soldiers of the United States in the Wars of 1775-1812, 1861-65
author: Joseph T. Wilson
blurb: A veteran of the 54th Massachusetts records the service of Black soldiers in the Revolution, the War of 1812 and the Civil War: recruiting, campaigns, Fort Pillow, rosters and schools.

title: Men of Mark: Eminent, Progressive and Rising
author: William J. Simmons
blurb: William J. Simmons, president of the State University at Louisville, gathers the lives of 177 Black men, from Crispus Attucks, Benjamin Banneker and Toussaint L'Ouverture to the ministers, teachers, lawyers, editors, inventors and public men of his own day, among them Frederick Douglass, Robert Smalls, Granville T. Woods and Alexander Crummell, with an introduction by Bishop Henry M. Turner.

title: A School History of the Negro Race in America, from 1619 to 1890, with a Short Introduction as to the Origin of the Race; Also a Short Sketch of Liberia
short: A School History of the Negro Race in America
author: Edward A. Johnson
blurb: Written for the children of the race by a teacher of eleven years, a history of the Negro in America from the first slaves landed in Virginia in 1619 through the colonies, the Revolution and the War of 1812, the struggle against slavery, Negro soldiers in the Civil War and the progress made since freedom, with sketches of noted Negroes and of Liberia.

title: The Suppression of the African Slave-Trade to the United States of America, 1638-1870
short: The Suppression of the African Slave-Trade
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
blurb: Du Bois's Harvard dissertation traces colonial, state, national and international efforts to suppress the African slave trade to the United States, 1638 to 1870, with chronological appendices of legislation.

title: The Tragedy of the Negro in America. A Condensed History of the Enslavement, Sufferings, Emancipation, Present Condition and Progress of the Negro Race in the United States of America
short: The Tragedy of the Negro in America
author: P. Thomas Stanford
blurb: P. Thomas Stanford, born a slave and later a pastor in Birmingham, England, and in Boston and Haverhill, tells the history of the Negro in America from the African slave trade through slavery, John Brown and emancipation to the progress since freedom, and condemns the lynchings of his own day.

title: Frederick Douglass: A Biography
author: Charles W. Chesnutt
blurb: A short life of Frederick Douglass by the novelist Charles W. Chesnutt: slavery in Maryland, escape, the anti-slavery platform, his newspaper, and public office after the war.

title: The Facts of Reconstruction
author: John R. Lynch
blurb: John R. Lynch, once Speaker of the Mississippi House and a congressman, recounts Reconstruction in Mississippi, the election of Revels and Bruce to the Senate, the overthrow of the state’s Republican government, and national politics through the convention of 1900.

title: Progress and Achievements of the Colored People: Containing the Story of the Wonderful Advancement of the Colored Americans—the Most Marvelous in the History of Nations—Their Past Accomplishments, Together with Their Present-Day Opportunities and a Glimpse into the Future for Further Developments—the Dawn of a Triumphant Era; A Handbook for Self-Improvement Which Leads to Greater Success
short: Progress and Achievements of the Colored People
author: Kelly Miller and Joseph R. Gay
blurb: A subscription handbook of self-improvement for Colored Americans: sketches of leaders and of openings in business, the professions and government service, chapters arguing that ancient Ethiopia and Egypt were Black civilizations, maxims for success, a survey of Negro schools compiled from Bureau of Education figures, and advice on rearing children and on health.

title: The Negro
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
